title: The frontal defence
summary: King cut off from the pawn: the rook goes in front of it, checks from the front or offers itself for a trade.
part.front.title: Checks from the front
part.front.summary: The king cut off, the rook on the first rank and the checks the black king cannot escape.
part.trade.title: The rook trade
part.trade.summary: When the checks are not enough, the rook offers itself. And the rule of three: when the pawn is already too close.
part.files.title: The pawn's file
part.files.summary: A knight pawn draws, a bishop pawn is dangerous: it comes down to how much room the black king has to hide.
part.king.title: Where the king stands
part.king.summary: Your king off the pawn's rank, and close enough that the black rook cannot cut it off for good.
part.recap.title: Summary
part.recap.summary: The rules of the frontal defence and the practical challenge.
step.t_front: The black king is on h5, next to its pawn, and the black rook on f7 cuts your king off: it cannot cross to the f-file. You defend with White. How do you hold this pawn?
step.t_front.hint1: Your rook is far from the pawn, on the first rank. That distance is a weapon.
step.t_front.hint2: Checks do not have to come from the side. They can come from the front, along the h-file and the g-file.
step.intro: This is the frontal defence. Your king is cut off and cannot get in front of the pawn. The rook does the defending: it stands on the first rank, in front of the pawn, and checks from the front. Look at the three empty squares between the rook and the pawn: g4, g3 and g2. That is the rule of three. With that much distance, the black king can neither approach the rook nor hide behind its pawn.
step.d_checks: Watch the checks. The black king tries to come forward and the rook will not let it.
step.d_checks.m1: Rh1+. A check from the front, along the h-file. The king has to move.
step.d_checks.m2: Kg4: the king steps in front of its own pawn. It is the only way to stay close to it.
step.d_checks.m3: Rg1+. Now along the g-file. In front of the pawn, the king gets checked too.
step.d_checks.m4: Kh4: back to the h-file, still touching the pawn.
step.d_checks.m6: Kg3: the king comes down, trying to reach the rook.
step.d_checks.m7: Rg1+. And it never ends: the pawn cannot advance while the king is in check, and the king cannot reach the rook, which is far away.
step.checks: Your turn. Give the checks from the front. And watch out: if the black king abandons the pawn to escape, the rook takes it.
step.checks.hint: Rh1+, then Rg1+. If the king goes to h3, the pawn on g5 is left undefended.
step.checks.done: The king ran to h3 and the pawn fell. A draw. That is what happens when the king gets tired of the checks.
step.t_emms: Now the pawn is a bishop pawn. The rook is in front, your king cut off along the e-file. Your move. Are the frontal checks enough here? If not, what else can the rook do?
step.t_emms.hint1: Imagine Black were to move. Where would the black king go?
step.t_emms.hint2: Sometimes the best square for the rook is one where it can be traded. Think about the king and pawn ending that would be left.
step.emms: If Black were to move here, Kg5! would win. With a bishop pawn the black king has more room to hide from the checks, and when they run out the black rook comes to e5 to guard the pawn from the side. The king steps out of the way and the pawn rolls down. The position is from Emms. With White to move there are two ways: Kd3, bringing the king closer, or Re1!, offering the trade. Let's look at the trade.
step.d_trade: Back to the knight pawn. The black rook cuts your king off. What if your rook offers itself?
step.d_trade.m1: Rf1. The rook faces the black rook. If Black trades, it is king and pawn against king.
step.d_trade.m3: Kxf1. The cut is gone: your king is free.
step.d_trade.m4: Kf5. The black king comes to support the pawn.
step.d_trade.m5: Kg1! Straight in front of the pawn.
step.d_trade.m7: Kf2: the opposition. The black king cannot get through. A drawn pawn ending.
step.rule3: And when none of this works? Here the pawn has come down one square, and between it and your rook only g3 and g2 are left. Black to move wins: the king shelters behind its pawn and the rook is too close for checks. It is the rule of three the other way round. With the pawn on its fifth rank, the frontal defence is over.
step.five: Same position, but now it is your move. Checks will not save you. One thing does.
step.five.hint: Rf1: offer the trade. Then Kxf1 and, when the black king comes, Kg2.
step.five.done: King in front of the pawn, with the opposition. A draw. The trade only works because your king was right there to recapture.
step.t_bpawn: A knight pawn, and your king is cut off by two files. Black threatens b4. What is the first move?
step.t_bpawn.hint1: Before giving check, the rook has to be in its place.
step.t_bpawn.hint2: In this defence the rook's place is always the same: in front of the pawn, on the first rank.
step.bishop: Compare it with a bishop pawn, your king cut off by the same two files. Black to move wins. The black king has room on both sides of the pawn to escape the checks, and your rook runs out of squares.
step.knight: With a knight pawn it is different. On the far side there is only the a-file: the black king has nowhere to hide. That is why the knight pawn draws even with the king cut off by two files, as Chéron already showed in 1923. The order of danger: bishop pawn, then centre pawn, then knight pawn. The rook pawn almost always draws.
step.getFront: Now you play. Rook in front of the pawn first; checks after.
step.getFront.hint: Rb1. Then Ra1+ when the king goes to a5, Rb1+ when it goes to b4, and Rc1+ when it goes to c4.
step.getFront.done: The black king walks from side to side and the pawn does not move. A draw.
step.t_rank: The rook is already in front of the pawn. But your king is badly placed. What is the move?
step.t_rank.hint1: Look at your king's rank and the pawn's rank.
step.t_rank.hint2: A rook does not only cut along a file. It cuts along a rank too.
step.rank: Kd4 was the only move. See what happens if you wait with Rb2: Rc4! The black rook cuts your king off along the fourth rank. It is stuck up there, the pawn comes down and the black king comes with it. A king on the pawn's rank invites that cut. Step down first.
step.farKing: The other king mistake is being too far away. Here your king is on c2, far from the pawn's file. If the rook goes straight in front of the pawn, Black plays Rd7 and cuts your king off by one more file: then there is no defence. King first: Kd3.
step.far: King first, rook after. Your move.
step.far.hint: Kd3. Then Rh1+ and Rg1+ as the black king moves.
step.far.done: The king arrived in time and the checks do the rest. A draw.
step.recap: The rules of the frontal defence. One: rook on the first rank, in front of the pawn, with three squares between them. Two: checks from the front; if the king abandons the pawn, take the pawn. Three: when the pawn ending that is left is a draw, offer the trade.
step.when: And when do you use it? When your king is cut off from the pawn and the pawn has not yet passed its fourth rank. With a knight pawn it holds with up to two files of cut-off; with a bishop or centre pawn only one, and even then not always. And your king: off the pawn's rank and close enough.
step.quick: One last one before the machine. The rook is in the wrong place.
step.quick.hint: Rg1, in front of the pawn. Then the checks, and Rxg5 if the king abandons the pawn.
step.quick.done: Rook in front, checks, and the pawn fell. A draw.
step.finish: Now the practical challenge. Rook in front of the pawn, checks from the front, and the trade when the pawn ending is a draw.
ex.e11: White to play and draw. Your rook is far away on the eighth rank, and the black rook cuts your king off along the f-file. Only one move holds.
ex.e11.hint: A check from behind does not scare this king. Where does the rook hold a knight pawn?
ex.e11.solution: Ra1! The rook goes back to the first rank, in front of the pawn, and from there the checks never end: Kg4 Rg1+, Kh4 Rh1+. Rh8+? loses: the black king hides and the pawn moves. Position from emanuelrigelnuma's study on Lichess.
ex.e12: White to play and draw. From Capablanca's analysis: the pawn has reached its fourth rank and your rook is on h2, not in front of it. The checks lose.
ex.e12.hint: Two ideas hold: drive the black rook off the d-file, or allow the pawn ending, which is a draw.
ex.e12.solution: Rd2, offering the trade: after Rxd2 Kxd2, your king gets in front of the pawn. Kc2, attacking the rook, also holds. Re2+? or Rh6+? lose: the black king walks out of the checks and the pawn advances with the black rook cutting your king off. Capablanca, as quoted on Wikipedia.
ex.e08: White to play and draw. A bishop pawn on its fifth rank, your king cut off along the d-file. The rook in front of the pawn no longer works.
ex.e08.hint: The rook cuts too. Think about separating the black king from its pawn, and then about who gets there first.
ex.e08.solution: Rh5! The rook cuts the black king off along the fifth rank. The pawn goes down on its own: c3, Ke2! (the only move), c2 and Rh1 (the only move), and your king reaches it. Ke2 at once also holds. What loses is putting the rook in front of the pawn: Rc1? Kc5, and the black king escorts the pawn. The idea comes from Yuri61's study.
ex.e13: White to play and draw. A central pawn, and your rook is already in front of it. Waiting loses.
ex.e13.hint: First drive the black king away from the pawn. Then, every move, ask: check, or back in front of the pawn?
ex.e13.solution: Rf1+! Kg4 and Re1: the rook goes back in front of the pawn (Rg1+? loses). Kf4 Rf1+, Ke4 Re1+ and, when the king abandons the pawn with Kf3, Rxe5. Every move is the only one: check when the king leans on the pawn, go back when it steps away.
ex.e14: White to play and draw. A bishop pawn, and the black rook on e5 cuts your king off. From Emms's position, with the analysis in GothamMath's study on Lichess.
ex.e14.hint: Your king cannot stay far from the e-file. What does the black rook have to watch?
ex.e14.solution: Kd4! The king attacks the rook and wins the tempo it needs. Re4+ Kd3: the king stays close, and the black rook has gone back in front. Now the checks: Kg4 Rg1+, Kf3 Rf1+. Every move is the only one. Any other first move loses: your king stays too far and the black rook has time.
ex.e15: White to play and draw. A knight pawn, your king cut off by two files. Chéron, 1923: with a central pawn this would lose. Here the black king's lack of room saves you, if you find the moves.
ex.e15.hint: Your king wants to get close to the c-file, and the rook stays in front of the pawn. When the black rook offers itself, look at what is left.
ex.e15.solution: Ke4! (the only move) Kc6 Rc1+ (Ra1, Re1, Rf1, Rg1 and Rh1 also hold) Rc5 Rb1! Rc3 Kd4! Ra3 Rc1+ Kb6 Rc3! The rook offers itself: if Rxc3, your king takes and the knight pawn does not get through. Chéron's position, 1923, as quoted on Wikipedia.
key.front: Knight pawn, white king cut off by one file: the white rook goes in front of the pawn and checks from the front, or offers a trade. A draw, whoever moves.
key.emms: Bishop pawn, same distance: here it depends on the move. With Black to play, the black king marches forward and wins; with White to play, the defence still arrives in time.
key.bpawn: White king cut off by two files: the rook goes in front of the pawn and from there checks without stopping. Only that route holds.
key.rank: The white king has to stand on the rank the pawn wants to advance to. On any other square the black rook cuts him off and the pawn walks on.
key.capa: The white rook is far from the pawn, but still in time: it starts checking right now and does not stop until it is in front of the pawn.
history: When the defending king is cut off from the pawn, it cannot stop the pawn by itself, and the rook has to do the job: it goes in front of the pawn and checks from the front, or offers itself for a trade at the right moment. It is one of the classical defences against rook and pawn, and it works better against some pawns than others: against a knight pawn it usually holds, against a bishop pawn it depends on who is to move. André Chéron was already showing this in 1923, and Edmar Mednis and John Emms set out the practical rules in more recent books. Capablanca showed the other side: if the rook arrives late, the checks no longer help.
practice: Practical challenge: a knight pawn, your king cut off by one file. Rook in front of the pawn, checks from the front and the trade at the right moment. The goal is a draw.
